newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany talks tough on anti-nuclear protesters.
newsitem.headline: Germany talks tough on anti-nuclear protesters.

text.p: German Interior Minister Manfred Kanther said on Thursday he would not shrink from a test of strength if it was forced on him by anti- nuclear activists opposing a shipment of nuclear waste.
Kanther said supporters of the anti-nuclear movement, including key members of opposition parties, knew they were indirectly provoking violence by calling for resistance

"The government will not be brought to its knees by violence," Kanther told parliament in a debate. "The government wants no test of strength between perpetrators of violence and the state, but we will not shy away if it comes to that."
Opposition politicians said Kanther was ignoring the concerns of ordinary people opposed to nuclear waste transport and committed to peaceful demonstrations.

"A clever state does not charge head-first through every wall that is put up before it," said Gerhard Glogowski, Social Democrat Interior Minister of Lower Saxony, where the controversial Gorleben nuclear waste depot is located.
"This shipment must be the last," he said.
Protests have heated up ahead of a shipment of nuclear waste due to arrive early next week at the medium-term storage site, east of Hanover.
Suspected anti-nuclear activists caused chaos on roads and railways in north Germany on Thursday, setting fire to signal boxes and setting traffic lights permanently on red.
In recent weeks, suspected activists have sabotaged rail lines, smashed windows of public buildings in Hamburg and daubed walls with anti-nuclear slogans.
In a sign of widespread local opposition, hundreds of children have occupied school halls to stop them being used to house police drafted in to guard the shipment.

Last year more than 19,000 police and border guards joined the biggest security operation in German peacetime history to get a shipment to Gorleben, and police fear protests will be even bigger this time.
Glogowski said 30,000 security officers would be needed to protect this shipment and said the operation would cost his state over 66 million marks ($39 million).
Joschka Fischer, parliamentary spokesman of the opposition Greens, called for nuclear power to be abandoned.

"The government is pushing through its nuclear energy policy like a police state. It is irresponsible to carry on with nuclear energy when we don't know what to do with the damned waste," he told parliament.
Fischer said Kanther's tough stance was an attempt to attract right-wing voters to the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) in Sunday's local election in the state of Hesse.

The head of the German police union, Hermann Lutz, appealed to demonstrators not to sacrifice police safety for their ideals. "Some of these people think the police are not human," Lutz told German television.
The latest delivery will include two rail containers from France and four more from German power plants, being moved together to save costs for the required security operation.
The convoy is due to be assembled near the Neckarwestheim power plant in south-west Germany on Friday and set off for Gorleben on Monday.
The district authorities in the Neckarwestheim area banned demonstrations along the route the nuclear waste will take on Friday from the power plant to a railway loading station.
($ = 1.687 German Marks)
